meta.subject: MICROECONOMICS
meta.author: bank-team-microeconomics
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify the divergence between private and social cost
questions.stem: During a nurse's handover, a factory beside the ward emits fumes; private cost is low but social cost is high. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The market overproduces because firms ignore external costs.
The market underproduces because external costs raise price.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the externality effect

options.text: Private and social costs are equal in competitive markets.
options.misconception: confuses private cost with social cost

options.text: External costs only matter for public goods, not factories.
options.misconception: limits externalities to public goods only

questions.explanation: Firms face only private cost, so output exceeds the social optimum. The tempting idea that external costs raise price confuses who bears them.
questions.hint: Compare private cost with social cost.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise when consumption creates external benefits
questions.stem: In a nurse's handover, a vaccination clinic run for staff shows benefits beyond the vaccinated worker. What is this called?

options.text: A negative production externality from clinic waste.
options.misconception: mislabels a benefit as a cost

options.text: A positive consumption externality from vaccination.
A common-resource overuse problem in staff time.
A public good with no exclusion possible.

questions.explanation: Vaccination protects others, so consumption yields external benefits. Labelling it a cost or common resource misidentifies the source.
questions.hint: Look for benefits beyond the buyer.

questions.learningObjective: State the relation social cost equals private plus external
questions.stem: A nurse's handover notes private cost 40 and external cost 15 for a procedure. What is social cost?
questions.explanation: Social cost equals private cost plus external cost, so 40 plus 15 is 55. Subtracting or ignoring the external part is the common slip.

questions.learningObjective: Compute overproduction when external costs are ignored
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives market output 120 and socially optimal output 90. How many units are overproduced?
questions.explanation: Overproduction is market output minus social optimum, 120 minus 90 equals 30. The gap arises because external costs are ignored.

questions.learningObjective: Set a Pigouvian tax equal to marginal external cost
questions.stem: A nurse's handover lists marginal external cost of 8 per unit. What Pigouvian tax internalises it?
questions.explanation: A Pigouvian tax equals marginal external cost at the optimum, here 8. A lower tax leaves overproduction; a higher one causes underproduction.
questions.hint: Match the tax to external cost.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why external costs create deadweight loss
questions.stem: A nurse's handover asks why unpriced pollution creates deadweight loss. Write a model answer.

answer.exemplar: When pollution is unpriced, firms produce beyond the social optimum, so units whose social cost exceeds social benefit are still made; that gap is the deadweight loss from external costs.

questions.explanation: The loss comes from units produced whose social cost exceeds social benefit. Pricing the externality removes those units and restores efficiency.
questions.hint: Focus on units beyond the optimum.

questions.learningObjective: Describe how a tax internalises an externality
questions.stem: A nurse's handover notes a tax on emissions shifted private cost up to social cost. What did the tax achieve?

options.text: It banned production of the polluting good.
It removed all external costs from society.
options.misconception: overstates what a tax can do

options.text: It created a new externality for downstream users.
It internalised the externality into private decisions.

questions.explanation: The tax makes firms face the full social cost, internalising the externality. It does not ban output or eliminate costs already incurred.

questions.topic: External benefits that grow with use
questions.learningObjective: Identify network-style external benefits
questions.stem: A nurse's handover tracks a messaging app whose value rises as more staff join. What externality is this?

options.text: A positive consumption externality that grows with use.
A negative consumption externality from screen time.
options.misconception: mislabels a benefit as a cost

options.text: A common-resource congestion problem.
A public good with no rival consumption.

questions.explanation: Value rising with users is a positive consumption externality. It is not congestion, which would reduce value, nor a pure public good.

questions.learningObjective: Size a subsidy to the marginal external benefit
questions.stem: A nurse's handover estimates marginal external benefit of 6 per dose. What subsidy aligns private and social benefit?
questions.explanation: A subsidy equal to marginal external benefit closes the gap, so 6. Too small leaves underconsumption; too large overconsumes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain underproduction from unpriced benefits
questions.stem: A nurse's handover asks why unpriced vaccination benefits cause deadweight loss. Write a model answer.

answer.exemplar: When vaccination benefits to others are unpriced, consumption falls below the social optimum, so units whose social benefit exceeds social cost are skipped; that shortfall is the deadweight loss.

questions.explanation: Underproduction occurs because private benefit understates social benefit. The missing units are those with social benefit above social cost.

questions.learningObjective: Use a price to reduce overuse of a congested facility
questions.stem: A nurse's handover notes parking is free and overcrowded at the hospital. Which policy fixes it?

options.text: A ban on all parking forever.
A subsidy for staff who drive.
A congestion charge on peak-hour parking.
Free bus passes for visitors only.

questions.explanation: Pricing peak use rations scarce space. Subsidies or bans are either backward or excessive.

questions.learningObjective: Compare cap-and-trade with a tax
questions.stem: A nurse's handover must choose between a tax and cap-and-trade for emissions. Which is true?

options.text: Neither affects the marginal cost of pollution.
A tax fixes quantity; cap-and-trade fixes price.
Both fix quantity and price together.
Cap-and-trade fixes quantity; a tax fixes price.

questions.explanation: Cap-and-trade sets total quantity and lets price vary; a tax sets price and lets quantity vary. Reversing them is the common error.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise inefficiency of uniform mandates
questions.stem: A nurse's handover compares a uniform emission cut with a market instrument. Which flaw is noted?

options.text: Taxes cannot reduce emissions at all.
Uniform cuts are always cheaper than taxes.
Uniform cuts ignore differing abatement costs.
Markets only work for private goods.

questions.explanation: A uniform mandate forces high-cost and low-cost abaters to cut equally, wasting resources. Market instruments exploit cost differences.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the Coase theorem to clear rights
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records a dispute over noise where rights are clear and bargaining is cheap. What outcome is predicted?

options.text: The outcome always favours the hospital.
Efficient outcome only if the polluter holds the right.
options.misconception: makes efficiency depend on rights holder

options.text: No bargain is possible without a tax.
Efficient outcome regardless of who holds the right.

questions.explanation: With clear rights and low transaction costs, parties bargain to efficiency. The initial rights holder only affects distribution.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why high transaction costs block Coase bargaining
questions.stem: A nurse's handover asks why many affected parties prevent Coase bargaining. Write a model answer.

answer.exemplar: With many affected parties, transaction and coordination costs are high, so private bargaining fails and a policy instrument such as a tax or regulation is needed instead.

questions.explanation: High transaction costs stop the bargain even with clear rights. That is when policy instruments become necessary.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a good as public by nonrivalry and nonexclusion
questions.stem: A nurse's handover lists a lighthouse visible to all ships. How is it classified?

options.text: A private good with full excludability.
A public good, nonrival and nonexcludable.
A common resource with rivalry only.
options.misconception: confuses public good with common resource

options.text: A club good with exclusion possible.
options.misconception: confuses public good with club good

questions.explanation: A lighthouse is nonrival and nonexcludable, hence a public good. Common and club goods differ on one of those margins.

questions.learningObjective: Link free riding to underprovision of public goods
questions.stem: A nurse's handover notes street lighting is rarely funded privately. Why?

options.text: Demand for light is perfectly inelastic.
Street lights are rival and excludable.
Free riders benefit without paying, so private provision fails.
Private firms cannot produce electricity.

questions.explanation: Nonexcludability lets people benefit without paying, so private firms cannot charge enough. The other statements misstate facts.
questions.hint: Who pays if no one can be excluded?

questions.topic: Aggregating demand for a public good
questions.learningObjective: Sum willingness to pay vertically for public goods
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records willingness to pay 30 and 20 for a public good. What is aggregate demand at that quantity?
questions.explanation: Public good demand is summed vertically, 30 plus 20 equals 50. Horizontal summing is for private goods.

questions.topic: Cost sharing for a public good
questions.learningObjective: Split cost by willingness to pay
questions.stem: A nurse's handover sets total cost 100 shared by two users with willingness to pay 60 and 40. What is the first user's share?
questions.explanation: Shares follow willingness to pay, so the first user pays 60. Equal splitting would ignore benefit differences.

questions.learningObjective: Set provision where sum of marginal benefits equals marginal cost
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives sum of marginal benefits 12 and marginal cost 12 for a public good. Is provision efficient?
questions.explanation: Efficiency requires sum of marginal benefits to equal marginal cost, so the condition holds and the answer is 1 for yes. Any gap signals inefficiency.
questions.hint: Compare sum of benefits with cost.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a good as common by rivalry and nonexclusion
questions.stem: A nurse's handover describes an open-access fishery used by all boats. How is it classified?

options.text: A public good with no rivalry.
A common resource, rival and nonexcludable.
A private good with full exclusion.
A club good with easy exclusion.

questions.explanation: Open-access fisheries are rival and nonexcludable, hence common resources. Public goods lack rivalry; private goods have exclusion.

questions.learningObjective: Explain tragedy of the commons
questions.stem: A nurse's handover asks why an open-access pasture is overgrazed. Write a model answer.

answer.exemplar: Because no one owns the pasture, each herder ignores the cost imposed on others, so stocking exceeds the sustainable level and the resource is degraded.

questions.explanation: Nonexcludability means individual herders face only private benefit, leading to overuse. Ownership or quotas can correct it.
questions.hint: Who bears the cost of extra grazing?

questions.learningObjective: Identify property rights as a remedy for common-resource overuse
questions.stem: A nurse's handover seeks a fix for an overused commons. Which option assigns clear ownership?

options.text: Price ceilings on output.
A subsidy for more intensive use.
Removing all regulation entirely.
Assigning private property rights to the resource.

questions.explanation: Clear ownership aligns incentives and prevents overuse. Subsidies or deregulation worsen it; price ceilings miss the cause.

questions.learningObjective: Compare total benefits with total costs
questions.stem: A nurse's handover shows a project with benefits 500 and costs 420. Is it worth doing?

options.text: No, because costs are too high.
Yes, because benefits exceed costs.
Only if benefits exceed 600.
Cannot tell without a tax.

questions.explanation: When benefits exceed costs, the project adds net value. The threshold and tax objections are red herrings.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a benefit-cost ratio above one
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records a benefit-cost ratio of 1.3. What does it imply?

options.text: The project breaks even exactly.
Costs exceed benefits by 30 percent.
Benefits are 30 percent larger than costs.
Benefits equal costs times 0.3.

questions.explanation: A ratio of 1.3 means benefits are 1.3 times costs, 30 percent larger. Reversing or misreading gives the wrong sign.

questions.learningObjective: Define asymmetric information in a market
questions.stem: A nurse's handover describes sellers knowing more about quality than buyers. What is this?

options.text: An externality from health care.
Perfect competition with full information.
A monopoly price-setting problem.
Asymmetric information between parties.

questions.explanation: Unequal information is asymmetric information. It is not perfect competition, monopoly, or an externality.

questions.learningObjective: Explain adverse selection in a used-goods market
questions.stem: A nurse's handover asks why bad-quality used cars drive out good ones. Write a model answer.

answer.exemplar: Sellers know quality but buyers do not, so buyers offer an average price; good sellers withdraw, leaving lemons, and the market unravels.

questions.explanation: Information asymmetry lets low quality dominate. Signaling or warranties can restore trade.
questions.hint: Average price drives out good sellers.

questions.learningObjective: Define moral hazard after a transaction
questions.stem: A nurse's handover notes insured patients take less care after coverage begins. What is this?

options.text: Adverse selection before coverage.
Moral hazard from hidden action.
A signaling equilibrium in wages.
A price ceiling distortion.

questions.explanation: Hidden action after the contract is moral hazard. Adverse selection occurs before contracting.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish signaling from screening
questions.stem: A nurse's handover compares a degree as a signal with an employer test as screening. Which is correct?

options.text: Both are done by the government.
Signaling is done by the uninformed party; screening by the informed.
Signaling is done by the informed party; screening by the uninformed.
Neither changes market outcomes.

questions.explanation: The informed party signals; the uninformed party screens. Reversing roles is the common mistake.

questions.learningObjective: Select an instrument given transaction costs
questions.stem: A nurse's handover must pick a policy for a widespread externality with high transaction costs. What is best?

options.text: A subsidy to the polluter.
Private Coase bargaining.
No intervention at all.
A Pigouvian tax or regulation.

questions.explanation: High transaction costs rule out Coase bargaining, so a tax or regulation is appropriate. Doing nothing or subsidising pollution worsens outcomes.

questions.learningObjective: Compute social cost from private and external components
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives private cost 50 and external cost 10 for a batch. What is social cost?
questions.explanation: Social cost equals private plus external, 50 plus 10 equals 60. Ignoring or miscombining the components is the slip.

questions.learningObjective: Compute social benefit from private and external components
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records private benefit 20 and external benefit 5 for a dose. What is social benefit?
questions.explanation: Social benefit equals private plus external, 20 plus 5 equals 25. Ignoring the external part understates value.

questions.learningObjective: Compare private and social cost magnitudes
questions.stem: A nurse's handover lists private cost 30 and social cost 45. Which is larger and by how much?

options.text: Cannot compare without revenue.
Private cost is larger by 15.
They are equal.
Social cost is larger by 15.

questions.explanation: Social cost exceeds private cost by 15, the external cost. Reversing or equating them misreads the data.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the output gap from cost divergence
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives market output 200 and social optimum 150. What is overproduction?
questions.explanation: Overproduction is 200 minus 150 equals 50 units. The gap comes from ignoring external costs.

questions.learningObjective: Compute tax revenue at a given tax
questions.stem: A nurse's handover sets a Pigouvian tax of 4 per unit on 80 units. What is tax revenue?
questions.explanation: Revenue is tax rate times quantity, 4 times 80 equals 320. Adding or reporting one factor is the slip.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the source of deadweight loss
questions.stem: A nurse's handover asks what creates deadweight loss from pollution. Which is correct?

options.text: Only units consumed by the firm.
All units produced by the firm.
Units produced whose social cost exceeds social benefit.
Units with zero private cost.

questions.explanation: Only units beyond the optimum, where social cost exceeds social benefit, create loss. Not all output is inefficient.

questions.learningObjective: Compute new private cost after tax
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives private cost 25 and a tax of 7. What is cost after internalisation?
questions.explanation: Internalised cost is private cost plus tax, 25 plus 7 equals 32, matching social cost. Forgetting the tax leaves 25.

questions.topic: External benefits that grow with use
questions.learningObjective: Compute network benefit at a given adoption
questions.stem: A nurse's handover values network benefit as 2 per user squared and adoption is 4. What is benefit?
questions.explanation: Benefit is 2 times 4 squared, 2 times 16 equals 32. Linear or cubic scaling misapplies the formula.

questions.learningObjective: Compute subsidy cost for a programme
questions.stem: A nurse's handover subsidises 50 doses at 6 each. What is total subsidy cost?
questions.explanation: Total subsidy is rate times quantity, 6 times 50 equals 300. Reporting only the rate or quantity is incomplete.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the shortfall from unpriced benefits
questions.stem: A nurse's handover asks what causes deadweight loss from underconsumption. Which is correct?

options.text: All units not consumed.
Units skipped whose social benefit exceeds social cost.
Units consumed at zero price.
Units with infinite private benefit.

questions.explanation: Only skipped units with social benefit above social cost create loss. Not all non-consumption is inefficient.

questions.learningObjective: Compute toll revenue from a congestion charge
questions.stem: A nurse's handover charges a 3 toll on 120 peak trips. What is toll revenue?
questions.explanation: Revenue is toll times trips, 3 times 120 equals 360. Adding or reporting one factor is the slip.

questions.learningObjective: Compute permit price from abatement costs
questions.stem: A nurse's handover sets total permits so the marginal abatement cost is 10. What is permit price?
questions.explanation: Under cap-and-trade, permit price equals marginal abatement cost at the cap, here 10. A different value signals disequilibrium.
questions.hint: Price equals marginal cost at cap.

questions.learningObjective: Compute total cost of a uniform mandate
questions.stem: A nurse's handover mandates 10 units of abatement costing 5 each. What is total cost?
questions.explanation: Total cost is unit cost times quantity, 5 times 10 equals 50. Adding or reporting one factor is the slip.

questions.learningObjective: Compute surplus split from a bargain
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records a bargain surplus of 40 split equally. What is each party's gain?
questions.explanation: Equal split gives 40 divided by 2 equals 20 each. Unequal splits would need stated shares.

questions.learningObjective: Compute net gain after transaction costs
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives gross bargain gain 30 and transaction cost 8. What is net gain?
questions.explanation: Net gain is gross gain minus transaction cost, 30 minus 8 equals 22. Adding or ignoring the cost is the slip.

questions.learningObjective: Compute aggregate demand for a public good
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records willingness to pay 25 and 15 for a public good. What is aggregate demand?
questions.explanation: Public good demand sums vertically, 25 plus 15 equals 40. Horizontal summing applies to private goods.

questions.learningObjective: Compute shortfall in private provision
questions.stem: A nurse's handover sets social optimum 100 and private provision 30 for a public good. What is the shortfall?
questions.explanation: Shortfall is optimum minus private provision, 100 minus 30 equals 70. Adding or reporting one factor is the slip.

questions.topic: Aggregating demand for a public good
questions.learningObjective: Compute individual share of aggregate demand
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records aggregate willingness to pay 60 from two users paying 35 and 25. What is the first user's share?
questions.explanation: The first user's share is their stated willingness to pay, 35. Equal splitting would ignore differences.

questions.topic: Cost sharing for a public good
questions.learningObjective: Compute total cost share across users
questions.stem: A nurse's handover lists shares 40 and 60 for a public good. What is total cost?
questions.explanation: Total cost is the sum of shares, 40 plus 60 equals 100. Subtracting or multiplying miscombines them.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the efficiency gap
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives sum of marginal benefits 10 and marginal cost 14 for a public good. What is the gap?
questions.explanation: The gap is benefits minus cost, 10 minus 14 equals negative 4, so provision is too high. A positive gap would mean too little.

questions.learningObjective: Compute sustainable yield
questions.stem: A nurse's handover estimates growth rate 0.1 times stock 500 for a fishery. What is sustainable yield?
questions.explanation: Sustainable yield is growth rate times stock, 0.1 times 500 equals 50. Adding or reporting one factor is the slip.

questions.learningObjective: Compute excess use beyond sustainable level
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records actual catch 80 and sustainable yield 50 for a fishery. What is excess use?
questions.explanation: Excess use is actual minus sustainable, 80 minus 50 equals 30. The excess depletes the stock.

questions.learningObjective: Compute gain from assigning rights
questions.stem: A nurse's handover values open-access yield 40 and private yield 70. What is the gain from rights?
questions.explanation: Gain from rights is private minus open-access yield, 70 minus 40 equals 30. Adding or reporting one value is the slip.

questions.learningObjective: Compute net benefit of a project
questions.stem: A nurse's handover lists benefits 600 and costs 450 for a project. What is net benefit?
questions.explanation: Net benefit is benefits minus costs, 600 minus 450 equals 150. Adding them would be meaningless.

questions.learningObjective: Compute benefit-cost ratio
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives benefits 260 and costs 200. What is the benefit-cost ratio?
questions.explanation: The ratio is benefits divided by costs, 260 over 200 equals 1.3. Inverting or miscombining gives the wrong number.

questions.learningObjective: Compute average price in a lemons market
questions.stem: A nurse's handover records good car value 10000 and lemon value 4000 with equal shares. What is average price?
questions.explanation: Average price is the midpoint, (10000 plus 4000) divided by 2 equals 7000. Good sellers withdraw at this price.

questions.learningObjective: Compute share of lemons after withdrawal
questions.stem: A nurse's handover starts with 50 good and 50 lemon cars; good sellers withdraw. What share are lemons?

options.text: 0 percent
50 percent
100 percent
25 percent

questions.explanation: Once good sellers withdraw, only lemons remain, so share is 100 percent. Ignoring withdrawal leaves 50 percent.

questions.learningObjective: Compute expected loss under insurance
questions.stem: A nurse's handover estimates loss probability 0.2 and loss size 5000 under insurance. What is expected loss?
questions.explanation: Expected loss is probability times size, 0.2 times 5000 equals 1000. Adding them would be wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Compute net benefit of a signal
questions.stem: A nurse's handover gives wage premium 2000 and signaling cost 1200. What is net benefit?
questions.explanation: Net benefit is premium minus cost, 2000 minus 1200 equals 800. Adding or reporting one factor is the slip.

questions.learningObjective: Compute deadweight loss reduction from a tax
questions.stem: A nurse's handover estimates deadweight loss 100 and a tax removes 60. What is remaining loss?
questions.explanation: Remaining loss is total minus removed, 100 minus 60 equals 40. Adding would be wrong.
